walls|en|City wall|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}}. == Examples of Fortified Cities (with Remaining Walls) == === Africa === * {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} === Europe === * [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}}. == Examples of Fortified Cities (with Remaining Walls) == === Africa === * {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} === Europe === * These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. {{ill|Naarden|en|Naarden|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naarden|qq=}}, Netherlands]] [[File:Munser1572.jpg|thumb|Map of {{ill|Paris|en|Paris|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Paris|qq=}}, 1572]] [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}}. == Examples of Fortified Cities (with Remaining Walls) == === Africa === * {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} === Europe === * Spain|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ávila|qq=}} * {{ill|Carcassonne|en|Carcassonne|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Carcassonne|qq=}} (France) * {{ill|Dubrovnik|en|Dubrovnik|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dubrovnik|qq=}} (Croatia) === Middle East === * {{ill|Aleppo|en|Aleppo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aleppo|qq=}} (Syria) * {{ill|Old City of Jerusalem|en|Old City of Jerusalem|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old City of Jerusalem|qq=}} === Asia === ; China * {{ill|Pingyao|en|Pingyao|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Pingyao|qq=}} * {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}} ; India * {{ill|Jaisalmer|en|Jaisalmer|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jaisalmer|qq=}} * (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers. Fortified cities typically featured {{ill|city gates|en|City gate|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city gates|qq=}}, moats, and {{ill|drawbridges|en|Drawbridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/drawbridges|qq=}}. Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In Africa, notable examples include {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} in ancient Egypt and {{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}}. == Examples of Fortified Cities (with Remaining Walls) == === Africa === * {{ill|Buhen|en|Buhen|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buhen|qq=}} === Europe === * Some cities added multiple layers of walls, with {{ill|watchtowers|en|Watchtower|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/watchtowers|qq=}} and {{ill|embrasures|en|Embrasure|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/embrasures|qq=}} for defense. Within the walls, fortifications often included {{ill|citadels|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadels|qq=}} where {{ill|nobles|en|Nobility|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/nobles|qq=}} resided, along with agricultural land and wells to sustain prolonged sieges. === Asia === In [[:en:China|China]], the original meaning of "城" (*cheng*, city) referred to the defensive walls that surrounded settlements. Later, it came to encompass the entire enclosed area. Chinese city walls often included {{ill|gatehouses|en|Gatehouse|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/gatehouses|qq=}} and multi-layered fortifications known as [[:en:Barbican|Oucheng]], which protected the gates. Examples of well-preserved city walls include those in {{ill|Nanjing|en|Nanjing|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanjing|qq=}} and {{ill|Xi'an|en|Xi'an|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Xi'an|qq=}}. In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}}, early fortified settlements like {{ill|Yoshinogari|en|Yoshinogari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshinogari|qq=}} during the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period|qq=}} featured moats and earthen walls, but these disappeared as centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō|en|Ritsuryō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō|qq=}} states developed. Later periods saw the emergence of {{ill|Walled City|lt=Walled City|lt=Castle towns|en|Castle town|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/castle towns|qq=}} like {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura|qq=}} and {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Edo|qq=}}, which were surrounded by moats and earthen walls. === Africa === In [[File:Exterior_of_great_enclosure,G.Zimbabwe.JPG|thumb|{{ill|Great Zimbabwe|en|Great Zimbabwe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Great Zimbabwe|qq=}} (World Heritage Site) in Zimbabwe]] '''Jōkaku Toshi''' (城郭都市, *Jōkaku Toshi*) refers to {{ill|fortified cities|en|Fortified city|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fortified cities|qq=}} that are enclosed and protected by {{ill|city walls|en|City wall|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/city walls|qq=}}Also referred to as '''城壁都市''' (*Jōheki Toshi*) or '''囲郭都市''' (*Ikaku Toshi*). In French: {{ill|ville fortifiée|fr|Ville fortifiée|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ville fortifiée|qq=}}, Cité fortifiée, or ville avec rempart; in English: walled city or fortified city; in German: befestigte Stadt.Sometimes called '''城塞都市''' (*Jōsai Toshi*), though in this case, '''{{ill|citadel|en|Citadel|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/citadel|qq=}}''' does not imply its literal English meaning.. Defensive structures such as {{ill|earthworks|en|Earthworks (engineering)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/earthworks|qq=}} and {{ill|moats|en|Moat|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moats|qq=}} were also utilized. == Overview == The history of fortified cities dates back to the {{ill|ancient civilizations|en|Ancient history|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient civilizations|qq=}} of {{ill|Egypt|en|Ancient Egypt|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt|qq=}}, {{ill|Mesopotamia|en|Mesopotamia|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mesopotamia|qq=}}, {{ill|Indus Valley|en|Indus Valley civilization|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Indus Valley|qq=}}, [[:en:China|China]], and {{ill|ancient Greece|en|Ancient Greece|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ancient Greece|qq=}}. The origins of fortified cities can be traced to {{ill|moated settlements|en|Moated site|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated settlements|qq=}}. These settlements emerged during the {{ill|Neolithic period|en|Neolithic|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Neolithic period|qq=}} with the advent of agriculture and were universally observed in many parts of the world. As wealth accumulated in agricultural settlements, they became targets for external threats. Early defensive measures included digging moats and building earthen mounds. These defenses evolved, with moats deepened and filled with water, and the construction of higher walls made of {{ill|rammed earth|en|Rammed earth|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/rammed earth|qq=}}, {{ill|bricks|en|Brick|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bricks|qq=}}, or {{ill|stone|en|Stone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone|qq=}}. Fortified cities developed primarily in regions where urban civilizations thrived, such as the {{ill|Middle East|en|Middle East|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle East|qq=}}, {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Europe|qq=}}, and [[:en:China|China]], where frequent conflicts occurred between tribes and nations. However, the high population density within fortified cities often led to poor sanitation and the rapid spread of diseases, especially in low-lying areas. === Europe === Many European cities originated as military encampments of the {{ill|Roman Empire|en|Roman Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Roman Empire|qq=}}. To the Romans, regions like {{ill|Gaul|en|Gaul|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gaul|qq=}} were considered barbaric frontiers. As the Roman Empire expanded, it established military bases known as *castra*, which served as both military outposts and accommodation facilities. These bases later evolved into cities after the Roman army departed, leaving a lasting imprint on European city names. For example, the suffix "caster" in {{ill|Lancaster|en|Lancaster, England|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lancaster|qq=}} or "chester" in {{ill|Manchester|en|Manchester|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Manchester|qq=}} derives from *castra*In Latin, "tra," or "tre" in French, is typically rendered as "ter" in English. English contains many French-origin words due to the historical rule of the Norman French over England.. Other examples include "-burg" from {{ill|Old High German|en|Old High German|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old High German|qq=}} for "fortress" (e.g., {{ill|Hamburg|en|Hamburg|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hamburg|qq=}}) and "-bury" in English (e.g., {{ill|Canterbury|en|Canterbury|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Canterbury|qq=}}). Similar patterns are observed in the Slavic term "{{ill|grad|en|Grad (fortification)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/grad|qq=}}" for "fortified city." Most major cities in continental Europe before the medieval period were surrounded by high walls. The capital of the {{ill|Byzantine Empire|en|Byzantine Empire|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Byzantine Empire|qq=}}, {{ill|Constantinople|en|Constantinople|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Constantinople|qq=}}, was fortified with three layers of walls over 10 meters high. Likewise, the central city of the {{ill|Islamic Golden Age|en|Islamic Golden Age|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Islamic Golden Age|qq=}}, {{ill|Baghdad|en|Baghdad|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Baghdad|qq=}}, was surrounded by circular walls with seven gates and a diameter of 2.35 kilometers.
